chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umeyr, from Jameel, and Ibn Bukayr, and Hammad ibn Usman, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:
The perpetrator of Zahaar, when he divorces, the expiation drops off from him.
ai.seo_question: Does divorce cancel the Zahaar expiation in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi clarifies that the ritual expiation (kaffarah) for Zahaar is contingent upon the marriage bond remaining intact; thus, if the husband divorces his wife, the obligation is lifted. This ruling highlights the juristic view that Zahaar is a specific impediment to marital intimacy rather than a permanent sin, distinguishing it from other forms of expiation. It reflects the practical legal reasoning found in Shia fiqh where the remedy is tied to the restoration of the marital state.

en.hubeali:
Ali Bin Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abu Umeyr, from Jameel, and Ibn Bukeyr, and Hammad Bin Usman, 
(It has been narrated) from Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> having said:
‘The perpetrator (committer) of the Zahaar, when he divorces, the expiation drops off from him’.
en.sarwar: 23. Ali ibn Ibrahim has narrated from his father from ibn abu ‘Umayr from Jamil an ibn Bukayr and Hammad ibn ‘Uthaman who has said the following: “Abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, has said, ‘

If one who has expressed al-Zihar (calling one’s wife as one’s mother) about his wife, divorces her then expiation cancels out and it no more is applicable to his case.’” Ali ibn Ibrahim has said that if a man divorces his wife or takes his slave-girl out of his possession he then does not owe expiation of al-Zihar unless he goes back to his wife and returns his slave-girl into his possession. When he does so then it is not proper for him to go near them without paying the expiation.
